column2: On S={1,2,3,4,5,6}, R contains all diagonal pairs and exactly the additional pairs (1,2),(2,1),(2,3),(3,2),(4,5),(5,4). What is the minimum number of ordered pairs that must be added to make R an equivalence relation with exactly two equivalence classes?
column8:
Answer: (B) Six ordered pairs.
Given: R is already reflexive and symmetric; the chains force 1,2,3 into one class and 4,5 into another.
Formula/Principle: An equivalence class of size s contains all \(s^2\) ordered pairs; merging classes of sizes a,b adds \(2ab\) cross-pairs.
Step 1: Complete transitivity in \(\{1,2,3\}\) by adding (1,3) and (3,1). The minimal closure then has classes of sizes 3,2,1.
Step 2: Exactly two classes requires merging at least two of these components; splitting a forced component is impossible.
Step 3: The possible additional merge costs are \(2(3)(2)=12\), \(2(3)(1)=6\) and \(2(2)(1)=4\).
Step 4: Merge \(\{4,5\}\) with \(\{6\}\), giving total additions \(2+4=6\).
Worked derivation: \[N_{\min}=2+\min\{12,6,4\}=6.\]
Why: Completing transitivity alone leaves three classes and therefore does not satisfy the extra class-count condition. Comparing merge costs proves that the chosen six additions are sufficient and minimal, not just one possible completion.
Why not the others: (A) stops at the three-class closure; (C) merges the size-three and size-one components; (D) merges the two largest components.
Key point: Establish forced classes, then optimise the permitted mergers.
